headline: Can AI agents design real circuits yet? New benchmark measures AI-generated electronics
summary: EEBench, a new physics-graded benchmark, evaluates the quality of AI-designed circuits by simulating real-world component tolerances and performance.
details: OpenAI has demonstrated GPT-6 Astra's ability to work with circuit board designs in KiCad, sparking questions about how to measure the quality of AI-generated electronics.
While AI models have access to vast amounts of technical knowledge, their output in conventional design tools often doesn't reflect this understanding.

EEBench utilizes atopile, allowing AI agents to directly manipulate components, connections, and electrical constraints in code. This enables iterative design, simulation, and testing within the project environment.

A key task in EEBench involves designing a circuit for an energy meter that must maintain processor power for 20ms during a 5V supply outage, testing the AI's ability to select appropriate components like capacitors.
EEBench goes beyond nominal values by simulating real-world component tolerances, voltage-dependent capacitance, and other factors that can cause designs to fail.
The benchmark also includes harder analog tasks, such as synthesizing a multiple-feedback low-pass filter, requiring the AI to solve for component ratios and meet strict performance limits.

Crucially, EEBench uses actual manufacturer parts with specifications extracted from datasheets, forcing AI agents to balance electrical performance, cost, and supply chain considerations—a true reflection of real-world hardware design.
Each EEBench check is deterministic, building the design, generating a bill of materials, and running SPICE simulations to measure performance against specified limits.
caption:
AI is getting better at designing circuits, but how do we know if they're actually any good? A new benchmark called EEBench aims to find out.

OpenAI has demonstrated GPT-6 Astra's ability to work with circuit board designs in KiCad, sparking questions about how to measure the quality of AI-generated electronics.

While AI models have access to vast amounts of technical knowledge, their output in conventional design tools often doesn't reflect this understanding.

EEBench utilizes atopile, allowing AI agents to directly manipulate components, connections, and electrical constraints in code. This enables iterative design, simulation, and testing within the project environment.

A key task in EEBench involves designing a circuit for an energy meter that must maintain processor power for 20ms during a 5V supply outage, testing the AI's ability to select appropriate components like capacitors.

EEBench goes beyond nominal values by simulating real-world component tolerances, voltage-dependent capacitance, and other factors that can cause designs to fail.

The benchmark also includes harder analog tasks, such as synthesizing a multiple-feedback low-pass filter, requiring the AI to solve for component ratios and meet strict performance limits.

Crucially, EEBench uses actual manufacturer parts with specifications extracted from datasheets, forcing AI agents to balance electrical performance, cost, and supply chain considerations—a true reflection of real-world hardware design.

Each EEBench check is deterministic, building the design, generating a bill of materials, and running SPICE simulations to measure performance against specified limits.
